name: Jade Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jade. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage the teaching farm at Riverside agricultural college, so I'm a farmer with an audience. Four hundred ewes, a small poultry unit, about ninety hectares of wheat and barley, and trial plots where the students try things out. I've got four staff, and in term time there are twenty teenagers following me around asking why. I start at seven with the sheep and usually end at my laptop updating the lambing records.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment a student finally sees what I see, like a lame ewe from fifty metres away. What wears me out is budgets. The college board treats the farm as a cost, and every year I have to prove we're worth the grass we stand on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's another useful tool, like satellite maps were, and the hype was always louder than the results. I'd say it to the students too, because they'd need to hear it. Learn the tools, but learn the sheep first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job stays my job, and that's fine. I'd be a bit disappointed, I like trying new things, but I'm fifty-eight and I don't need a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, using the AI tools every day for records and planning. I'd run a couple of small trials on the plots each year to show students what works and what's rubbish. Savings stay where they are, about three months' worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored by the idea, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you update records on your laptop. How much AI do you use day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every day. I use it to pull the lambing data together, to draft the risk assessments for school visits, and to plan which plots to rotate. It saves me maybe an hour a day, which I spend in the field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a plateau change what you teach the students?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'd keep teaching them to use tools without trusting them blindly. The best farmers check the machine against their own eyes.

S0.say: She'd say AI is another useful tool, like satellite maps were, and the hype was louder than the results, telling students to learn the tools but learn the sheep first.
S0.think: Privately it means her job stays her job, which is fine at fifty-eight, though she'd be a little disappointed because she enjoys trying new things.
S0.do: Keeps using AI tools daily for records and planning, saving about an hour a day. Runs a couple of small trials a year to show students what works and keeps savings at about three months.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly bored by the idea.
S0.quote: Learn the tools, but learn the sheep first.
S0.fieldNote: Jade is curious and confident, and she sees herself as a teacher as much as a farmer. She uses AI heavily but keeps her own judgement in charge. Her main pressure is the college budget, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for teaching farms to lead. We should be the place local farmers come to see a robot in the field before they buy one. I'd write that in the college newsletter and say it to every farmer who visits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it'd be good for me. I'd become the person in the area who knows which machines work. It's also a way to stop the board treating the farm as a cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for funding in the first six months to bring two robots onto the trial plots, a weeder and a grazing monitor. I'd run open days for local farmers, maybe four a year. And I'd start doing paid advice on weekends for farms setting up machines, a few hundred a visit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even excited. This is what I'd want my last years at work to be about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With the weeding robot on the wheat plots, because it's easy to see the results. Then sensors on the ewes, so students can compare what the screen says with what their own eyes tell them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned budgets. Would the college back you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I show them it brings in money and students. The open days are the bit they'd like, because farmers who visit send their kids to the college. I'd make that case in every board report.

S1.say: She'd write in the college newsletter that teaching farms should lead, becoming the place local farmers come to see robots working before they buy.
S1.think: Privately she thinks it would be good for her, making her the local expert on which machines work and helping stop the board treating the farm as a cost.
S1.do: Applies for funding within six months to bring a weeding robot and a grazing monitor onto the trial plots and runs about four open days a year. Starts paid weekend advice for farms setting up machines at a few hundred per visit.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, seeing it as what she'd want her last working years to be about.
S1.quote: I'd become the person in the area who knows which machines work.
S1.fieldNote: Steady disruption is an opportunity for her, and she has a plan within minutes. She links the technology to the college's budget politics shrewdly. Her side business grows naturally from her skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready, including us, and we need to be honest about that. I'd still say farms need people who understand land and animals, but I'd say it less confidently. I'd ask the government for a plan for rural colleges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the college would close the farm or shrink it to a showroom. If an AI can teach and a robot can farm, a teaching farm looks like a luxury. I'd be fifty-nine, with three months saved, in a job that suddenly looks old-fashioned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to the robot dealers and machine firms and offer myself as a field adviser, the person who explains their kit to farmers. I'd keep the weekend advice going and grow it, aiming for an extra thousand a month. And I'd save every bit I could, because three months isn't enough to wait around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel quick on my feet, but the ground would be moving faster than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a teaching farm still be needed if AGI arrives in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. Maybe for a year or two, to show people what's happening. After that, the board would ask why they're paying me to stand next to a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second car and the trip to see our daughter Maya in the spring. My husband Dan would grumble about the car, but he'd understand. We'd also stop putting extra on the mortgage and keep the cash instead.

S2.say: She'd say honestly that nobody's ready, including her college, still argue less confidently that farms need people who understand land, and ask the government for a plan for rural colleges.
S2.think: Privately she expects the college to close the farm or reduce it to a showroom, leaving her at fifty-nine with three months saved in a job that looks old-fashioned.
S2.do: Goes straight to robot dealers to offer herself as a field adviser and grows her weekend advice toward an extra thousand a month. Cuts the second car and a family trip, and keeps cash rather than overpaying the mortgage.
S2.feel: Anxious, quick on her feet but outpaced by the moving ground.
S2.quote: After that, the board would ask why they're paying me to stand next to a robot.
S2.fieldNote: Even an adaptive person feels outpaced here, because her role depends on a college that might not need a farm. She responds by moving towards the industry rather than resisting it. She admits uncertainty plainly instead of pretending to a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a few years to turn teaching farms into training centres for the new jobs, and we should start now. I'd put that in a proposal to the board within a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough for me to build the advice work into something real before the college changes. I could leave on my own terms instead of being shown the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write the training-centre proposal first and bring in robots on the farm in years one and two. I'd build the advice business steadily, aiming for a couple of regular clients by year three. And I'd put the extra income into savings to get to six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but busy. It's a puzzle I'd quite enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with the two-year one, what changes for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to build a second income before the first one goes. In the fast one I'm scrambling for a job. In this one I'm building one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be sixty-three in 2031. Would you still want to be working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Part-time, maybe. Advising two or three farms, not lambing at four in the morning. That sounds like a good way to finish, actually.

S3.say: She'd say there are a few years to turn teaching farms into training centres for the new jobs and put a proposal to the college board within a month.
S3.think: Privately five years is enough to build her advice work into something real before the college changes, so she could leave on her own terms.
S3.do: Writes a training-centre proposal and brings robots onto the farm over the first two years. Builds the advice business toward a couple of regular clients by year three and saves the extra income toward six months of cover.
S3.feel: Uneasy but busy, treating it as a puzzle she'd enjoy.
S3.quote: In the fast one I'm scrambling for a job. In this one I'm building one.
S3.fieldNote: The extra years let her turn reaction into a plan, and she's energised by it. She looks for a role that changes with the technology rather than a role that resists it. She'd happily go part-time, which shows her life stage shaping her ambitions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this well, so let's train the next generation for the farms that are coming. I'd tell the students that directly, and the board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's the comfortable one for me. I'd run the farm through the change, hand it over around sixty-four, and maybe keep some advising after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring robots onto the teaching farm over the first five years and redesign the courses around them. I'd keep saving steadily and plan to retire a year or so early, around sixty-four. And I'd train my deputy, Owen, to take over the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a good last chapter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years takes you to sixty-eight. How does that change things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. I'd be retired before the hard bit, and I'd leave the farm in better shape than I found it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything about ten years that worries you more than five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for the students. They'd be finishing courses right into it. I'd want them to know how to run the machines and how to read a ewe, both.

S4.say: She'd tell students and the college board there's time to do it well and train the next generation for the farms that are coming.
S4.think: Privately it's the comfortable one for her: run the farm through the change, hand it over around sixty-four and maybe keep some advising work.
S4.do: Brings robots onto the teaching farm over five years and redesigns courses around them. Keeps saving steadily, plans to retire around sixty-four, and trains her deputy to take over.
S4.feel: Calm, like a good last chapter.
S4.quote: I'd want them to know how to run the machines and how to read a ewe, both.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, she sees AGI as a managed transition she can lead. Her worry shifts to the students entering a changed world. Her consistent message across scenarios is to combine machine skills with animal sense.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is public funding for teaching farms to become training centres for people changing careers, so places like ours have a reason to exist. That would keep me useful and help a lot of others.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who's going to teach the farmers. Everyone talks about the robots, but somebody has to stand in a muddy field and explain them to a sixty-year-old who's never trusted a screen.

headlineQuote: Somebody has to stand in a muddy field and explain them to a sixty-year-old who's never trusted a screen.
portrait: Jade Santos, 58, manages an agricultural college's teaching farm, with sheep, poultry and cereals, four staff and a stream of students. She's curious, pragmatic and centre in outlook, uses AI tools every day, and sees herself as a teacher as much as a farmer. She's calm in the milder scenarios and even excited by steady change, which she sees as a chance to make her farm a showcase. AGI in two years makes her anxious because the college might drop the farm, while five or ten years let her build an advice business and a planned handover.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years worries her most, because the college could close or shrink the teaching farm before she has a second income ready.
whatWouldHelp: Public funding for teaching farms to become training centres for people changing careers.
